name: Mugwort

lead: Mugwort refers to several Artemisia species used in food, folk medicine, moxibustion and, more recently, skincare billed as calming.
No human trials of mugwort skincare were found; evidence cited in sources is traditional use and preliminary lab findings.

paras: Extracts contain terpenes such as cineole, camphor and thujone, which preliminary studies associate with antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activity.

Mugwort pollen is a common allergen and the plant may trigger reactions in people sensitive to Asteraceae. Thujone is a neurotoxin at high concentrations, and herbal safety guidance advises against use in pregnancy.

lead: Mugwort is a common name for several aromatic Artemisia species: Artemisia vulgaris in Europe, and A. argyi (Chinese mugwort) or A. princeps (Korean ssuk, Japanese yomogi) in East Asia.[1] It has a long history in folk medicine, food, and moxibustion, and extracts are used in Korean skincare marketed as calming.[1][2]

Mugwort pollen is a major cause of hay fever and allergic asthma, and the plant typically contains thujone, which at high concentrations has been linked to seizures and abortive effects.[1] No published trials of mugwort skincare were found.
infobox: Artemisia vulgaris, A. argyi, A. princeps

paras: Mugwort has been used since at least the Iron Age as medicine, food and protective herb. Folk uses include for sleeplessness, menstrual cramps, and as an anthelminthic. Indigenous North American uses included washes for bruises, itching and sores.[1] In East Asia dried mugwort (moxa) is burned in moxibustion; a 2012 Cochrane review found it did not reduce breech presentation compared with placebo.[1]

Essential oil components include camphor, cineole, thujones, and borneol, and composition varies with species, habitat and season. Preliminary studies report antimicrobial, antifungal and anti-inflammatory properties of extracts.[1][2]

Mugwort pollen allergy is common in Northern Europe, North America and parts of Asia; the main allergen is Art v 1.[1] The Botanical Safety Handbook advises against use in pregnancy without medical supervision.[1] People sensitive to other Asteraceae plants may react.[2]

No studies found on mugwort as a skincare ingredient. Registered trials involving Artemisia concern pollen allergy diagnostics or immunotherapy (for example NCT01984541 and NCT07563439) and other Artemisia species for non-skin conditions.[3][4]
